## Motivation

Kubernetes service discovery cannot converge to the true pod set when the watch stream is unreliable, which is the normal operating condition on some managed providers: long-lived watches are dropped every few minutes and sometimes go **silently stale**, yielding neither events nor errors.

Three coupled defects in `service_discovery.rs`:

1. **Delete events are structurally lost.** The watch consumes `watcher(...).applied_objects()`, which yields only `Apply`/`InitApply` and discards `Delete`. A removal is caught only opportunistically, via an `Apply` carrying a `deletion_timestamp` during graceful termination. A pod that disappears while the watch is down, or is force-deleted, stays a registered worker forever — nothing reconciles against a fresh LIST, and the registry health checker only marks workers unhealthy, never deregisters.
2. **A silently stale watch disables the restart path.** When the stream neither yields nor errors (observed: 20+ minutes, zero watcher-error lines), `try_for_each` never returns, so the outer loop — the only place a fresh `watcher()` re-LIST could happen — never runs.
3. **The error-restart path stalls 60–360 s per reconnect**, sleeping `retry_delay` *plus* an unconditional `check_interval` every iteration.

## Change

`reconcile_from_list()`: a paged full LIST that feeds every selector-matching, non-terminating pod through the existing `handle_pod_event`, and removes every tracked pod no longer present via `handle_pod_deletion`. A pod with a `deletion_timestamp` counts as absent, mirroring the watch path watch-independently, so a draining pod stops receiving traffic even when the watch is dead. Any page failing aborts the pass before the removal phase, so a partial view can never drive removals.

Driven from a periodic timer (`--service-discovery-resync-secs`, default 30) and at the top of each watch (re)start; the redundant unconditional sleep is dropped so reconnects are prompt.

The tracked set is keyed by `pod.metadata.uid`, not by name. Under `Api::all` — the default, and what `gateway-cluster-scoped.yaml` ships — names are unique only per namespace, so a dead `ns-a/engine-0` stays tracked while `ns-b/engine-0` lives; and a pod replaced under one name is tracked alongside its predecessor instead of evicting it. The UID is stable across the status/readiness flips that make full-struct equality unusable, so it also lets `handle_pod_deletion` resolve by identity rather than exact-struct `HashSet::remove` (the fragility noted in #26842).

Two cases handled explicitly:

- A departed pod whose worker URL is claimed by a live healthy pod in the same LIST is a same-URL replacement (hostNetwork gives a pod its node's IP), so it is forgotten rather than deregistered.
- Membership in `tracked_pods` records that an AddWorker was *submitted*, not that it succeeded, and the add path short-circuits on tracked pods forever. A listed healthy pod that is tracked but absent from the registry is therefore forgotten so it is submitted again — via `find_workers_by_url`, since dp-aware workers register as `<url>@<rank>`, and gated on a per-URL in-flight check because `submit()` does not dedup.

## Relationship to #30270 and #26842

Both diagnose the same root causes and fix the **event handling**; this is complementary, adding the watch-independent periodic LIST that neither covers. When the watch is dead or silently stale — our dominant failure mode — better event handling has no events to handle.

Split out of this PR, independently reviewable: **#38523** (worker registry re-registration) and **#38524** (add/remove handoff race).

## Verification

`cargo test --lib` 410/410 (`service_discovery` 33 → 48); `cargo +nightly fmt --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all-targets` adds no new warnings. Every new test was confirmed to fail against the code it replaces.

Live on a 2-replica colocated cell behind 2 router replicas (managed k8s with frequent watch drops), steady 0.6 rps, isl 512 / osl 1200, full 2-pod rolling update with two cold starts, no external remediation:

| | client failures |
| -- | -- |
| stock router | **26** (12× 503, 4× 500, 10× connection errors) |
| this patch, resync 10 s | **0** across 2,156 requests |

Captured router logs show the reconcile doing what the watch could not: a dead pod removed on the periodic tick while that replica's watch was silently stale, and replacement pods registered on the tick boundary on both replicas (the stock router left a Ready pod unregistered for 12+ minutes in the same environment).

- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).

Cross-reference: I opened #37249, which removes one of the concrete causes of the state `forget_lost_registration` in this PR exists to recover.

`sgl-model-gateway` pins `wfaas = "=1.0.0"`, and in wfaas 1.0.0/1.0.1 a step that fails with `FailureAction::ContinueNextStep` is recorded in the tracker as `skipped` but signals `StepResult::Failure` to the scheduler. The scheduler enqueues a step's dependents only on `Success | Skip`, so nothing downstream ever runs and the workflow ends in the deadlock branch as `Failed`. In `create_local_worker_workflow()` that is `discover_metadata`, with `discover_dp_info` → `create_worker` → `register_workers` hanging off it — so one failing optional metadata fetch means the worker is never registered, while `handle_pod_event` has already inserted the pod into `tracked_pods` and only rolls that back when `submit()` itself fails.

That is exactly the class this PR's doc comment describes:

> Membership in `tracked_pods` records that an AddWorker job was SUBMITTED, not that it succeeded […] A job that fails after that […] only records a failed `JobStatus`, and nothing untracks the pod.

The causes named there (`detect_connection_mode` exhausting `worker_startup_timeout_secs`, a failing DP discovery, a workflow that never starts) are all comparatively rare. The wfaas one is not: a transient hiccup on a single optional HTTP call to a pod that has just started is enough to trigger it, so in practice it is a frequent producer of tracked-but-unregistered pods rather than an exotic one.

The two changes are complementary and independent, and can land in either order:

- **This PR without #37249** — the failure still happens on every occurrence; the reconcile recovers the pod, but only on a later resync tick.
- **#37249 without this PR** — that particular cause is gone, but an `AddWorker` failing for any other reason, and a pod whose event never arrives because the watch is dead or silently stale, are still unrecovered.

If it would be useful to reviewers, I am happy to extend `forget_lost_registration`'s doc comment here to name the wfaas case alongside the others once #37249's disposition is clear.

`present` is keyed on the bare pod name, but with no `--service-discovery-namespace` this is `Api::all`, where pod names are only unique **per namespace**. Same shape without namespaces involved: a pod replaced under the same name (StatefulSet / LeaderWorkerSet, or force-delete + recreate) with a new IP. The name is present, so the new `PodInfo` is added alongside the old one and the old one is never removed. It converges only if a tick happens to land in the window where the name is absent-or-terminating.

That test passes because step 3 waits for `worker_count == 0` before recreating the pod, which manufactures the empty window the name key needs.

The doc comment above is right that full-`PodInfo` equality is too strict. Name is just too loose in the other direction. `pod.metadata.uid` has both properties you want: stable across the status/readiness flips this comment is protecting against, and different for a recreated pod. Carrying a `uid` on `PodInfo` and building `present` from uids would also let `handle_pod_deletion` resolve the tracked entry by identity instead of exact-struct `HashSet::remove`, fixing the watch path's removal at the same time.

The new `fake_pod_api` scaffolding makes the regression test cheap: track `{name: p, ip: A}`, have the LIST return `{name: p, ip: B}`, assert A is gone.

+    /// Held for the duration of a pass so the two drivers never interleave.
+    lock: tokio::sync::Mutex<()>,
+    /// Consecutive failed passes, used only to escalate the log level.
+    consecutive_failures: AtomicU32,
+}

+/// Full LIST + reconcile of the tracked worker set against the API server.
+///
+/// Adds any healthy, selector-matching pod not yet tracked, and removes any
+/// tracked pod that has disappeared from the API server or begun terminating
+/// (mirroring the watch path's deletion_timestamp handling). This is the
+/// authoritative resync that makes worker correctness independent of
+/// watch-stream reliability: `.applied_objects()` drops Delete events and
+/// unstable environments drop the long-lived watch, so the watch alone
+/// cannot converge.
+///
+/// The LIST is paged; any page failing aborts the whole pass and leaves the
+/// worker set untouched, so a partial view can never drive removals.
+async fn reconcile_from_list(
+    pods: &Api<Pod>,
+    config: &ServiceDiscoveryConfig,
+    tracked_pods: Arc<Mutex<HashSet<PodInfo>>>,
+    app_context: Arc<AppContext>,
+    port: u16,
+    state: &ReconcileState,

+    // both call this, and letting two passes interleave lets the one holding
+    // the older LIST snapshot delete a pod the newer one has just added.
+    let _guard = state.lock.lock().await;
+    let started = time::Instant::now();

+    // already tracked at that instant are eligible for removal below. The
+    // watch runs concurrently, so a pod it registers while the LIST is in
+    // flight is legitimately missing from the response through no fault of
+    // its own. Removing it would open exactly the zero-worker window this
+    // reconcile exists to close, and the watch would not re-emit an Apply to
+    // repair it — the pod would stay unregistered until the next resync.

This dedup assumption holds only if membership in `tracked_pods` implies the worker actually reached the registry, and there's a path where it doesn't.

`handle_pod_event` inserts into `tracked_pods` and rolls back only when `submit()` itself fails (the `tracker.remove(pod_info)` at ~L613, i.e. channel closed/full). If the **job** fails afterwards -- `wait_for_completion` timing out (`worker_startup_timeout_secs` defaults to 1800s, `config/types.rs:514`), a failing activation step, a workflow-start error -- `record_job_completion` writes `JobStatus::failed` (`job_queue.rs:878`) and nothing else happens. `tracked_pods` is private to this file, so no other code can untrack it.

From then on this call is a permanent no-op: the pod is in `tracked_pods`, so `tracker.contains(pod_info)` short-circuits at L520 and the reconcile never retries. The pod stays absent from the registry while the reconcile believes it is registered -- the same unrecoverable state this PR closes on the delete side, still open on the add side. detail.body:
## Motivation

Kubernetes service discovery cannot converge to the true pod set when the watch stream is unreliable, which is the normal operating condition on some managed providers: long-lived watches are dropped every few minutes and sometimes go **silently stale**, yielding neither events nor errors.

Three coupled defects in `service_discovery.rs`:

1. **Delete events are structurally lost.** The watch consumes `watcher(...).applied_objects()`, which yields only `Apply`/`InitApply` and discards `Delete`. A removal is caught only opportunistically, via an `Apply` carrying a `deletion_timestamp` during graceful termination. A pod that disappears while the watch is down, or is force-deleted, stays a registered worker forever — nothing reconciles against a fresh LIST, and the registry health checker only marks workers unhealthy, never deregisters.
2. **A silently stale watch disables the restart path.** When the stream neither yields nor errors (observed: 20+ minutes, zero watcher-error lines), `try_for_each` never returns, so the outer loop — the only place a fresh `watcher()` re-LIST could happen — never runs.
3. **The error-restart path stalls 60–360 s per reconnect**, sleeping `retry_delay` *plus* an unconditional `check_interval` every iteration.

## Change

`reconcile_from_list()`: a paged full LIST that feeds every selector-matching, non-terminating pod through the existing `handle_pod_event`, and removes every tracked pod no longer present via `handle_pod_deletion`. A pod with a `deletion_timestamp` counts as absent, mirroring the watch path watch-independently, so a draining pod stops receiving traffic even when the watch is dead. Any page failing aborts the pass before the removal phase, so a partial view can never drive removals.

Driven from a periodic timer (`--service-discovery-resync-secs`, default 30) and at the top of each watch (re)start; the redundant unconditional sleep is dropped so reconnects are prompt.

The tracked set is keyed by `pod.metadata.uid`, not by name. Under `Api::all` — the default, and what `gateway-cluster-scoped.yaml` ships — names are unique only per namespace, so a dead `ns-a/engine-0` stays tracked while `ns-b/engine-0` lives; and a pod replaced under one name is tracked alongside its predecessor instead of evicting it. The UID is stable across the status/readiness flips that make full-struct equality unusable, so it also lets `handle_pod_deletion` resolve by identity rather than exact-struct `HashSet::remove` (the fragility noted in #26842).

Two cases handled explicitly:

- A departed pod whose worker URL is claimed by a live healthy pod in the same LIST is a same-URL replacement (hostNetwork gives a pod its node's IP), so it is forgotten rather than deregistered.
- Membership in `tracked_pods` records that an AddWorker was *submitted*, not that it succeeded, and the add path short-circuits on tracked pods forever. A listed healthy pod that is tracked but absent from the registry is therefore forgotten so it is submitted again — via `find_workers_by_url`, since dp-aware workers register as `<url>@<rank>`, and gated on a per-URL in-flight check because `submit()` does not dedup.

## Relationship to #30270 and #26842

Both diagnose the same root causes and fix the **event handling**; this is complementary, adding the watch-independent periodic LIST that neither covers. When the watch is dead or silently stale — our dominant failure mode — better event handling has no events to handle.

Split out of this PR, independently reviewable: **#38523** (worker registry re-registration) and **#38524** (add/remove handoff race).

`cargo test --lib` 410/410 (`service_discovery` 33 → 48); `cargo +nightly fmt --check` clean; `cargo clippy --all-targets` adds no new warnings. Every new test was confirmed to fail against the code it replaces.

`present` is keyed on the bare pod name, but with no `--service-discovery-namespace` this is `Api::all`, where pod names are only unique **per namespace**. So `ns-a/engine-0` being deleted while `ns-b/engine-0` is alive leaves `"engine-0"` in `present`, and the tracked entry for the dead pod is never returned by this filter. Nothing else deregisters it -- the registry health checker (`worker_registry.rs:646`) only calls `check_health_async()`, it never removes -- so that worker stays registered for the life of the process. `gateway-cluster-scoped.yaml` ships this configuration; `test_cross_namespace.py` uses distinct pod names (`cross-ns-worker-a`/`-b`), so it doesn't surface.

Same shape without namespaces involved: a pod replaced under the same name (StatefulSet / LeaderWorkerSet, or force-delete + recreate) with a new IP. The name is present, so the new `PodInfo` is added alongside the old one and the old one is never removed. It converges only if a tick happens to land in the window where the name is absent-or-terminating.

Worth flagging that `test_pd_type_change.py` is already written against exactly this scenario, and its docstring says it "covers the UID-based eviction path in handle_pod_event (same name, different UID) and the reconciliation diff (stale uid-A, missing uid-B)". But `grep uid src/service_discovery.rs` is empty on this branch and on `main` -- there is no uid anywhere. That test passes because step 3 waits for `worker_count == 0` before recreating the pod, which manufactures the empty window the name key needs.

The doc comment above is right that full-`PodInfo` equality is too strict. Name is just too loose in the other direction. `pod.metadata.uid` has both properties you want: stable across the status/readiness flips this comment is protecting against, and different for a recreated pod. Carrying a `uid` on `PodInfo` and building `present` from uids would also let `handle_pod_deletion` resolve the tracked entry by identity instead of exact-struct `HashSet::remove`, fixing the watch path's removal at the same time.

The new `fake_pod_api` scaffolding makes the regression test cheap: track `{name: p, ip: A}`, have the LIST return `{name: p, ip: B}`, assert A is gone.

This dedup assumption holds only if membership in `tracked_pods` implies the worker actually reached the registry, and there's a path where it doesn't.

`handle_pod_event` inserts into `tracked_pods` and rolls back only when `submit()` itself fails (the `tracker.remove(pod_info)` at ~L613, i.e. channel closed/full). If the **job** fails afterwards -- `wait_for_completion` timing out (`worker_startup_timeout_secs` defaults to 1800s, `config/types.rs:514`), a failing activation step, a workflow-start error -- `record_job_completion` writes `JobStatus::failed` (`job_queue.rs:878`) and nothing else happens. `tracked_pods` is private to this file, so no other code can untrack it.

From then on this call is a permanent no-op: the pod is in `tracked_pods`, so `tracker.contains(pod_info)` short-circuits at L520 and the reconcile never retries. The pod stays absent from the registry while the reconcile believes it is registered -- the same unrecoverable state this PR closes on the delete side, still open on the add side. (Pre-existing, but this pass is the natural place to repair it, and the "authoritative resync" framing invites the assumption that it already does.)

Since the pass is already paying for a full LIST, it seems worth reconciling against the registry rather than only the shadow set: treat "tracked but absent from `worker_registry`" as missing and resubmit. Use `find_workers_by_url(registry, url, dp_aware)` rather than `get_by_url` -- in dp-aware mode workers are registered as `<url>@<rank>`, so an exact-URL lookup never matches (same reason the new handoff guard reaches for it in `job_queue.rs`).

Cross-reference: I opened #37249, which removes one of the concrete causes of the state `forget_lost_registration` in this PR exists to recover.

`sgl-model-gateway` pins `wfaas = "=1.0.0"`, and in wfaas 1.0.0/1.0.1 a step that fails with `FailureAction::ContinueNextStep` is recorded in the tracker as `skipped` but signals `StepResult::Failure` to the scheduler. The scheduler enqueues a step's dependents only on `Success | Skip`, so nothing downstream ever runs and the workflow ends in the deadlock branch as `Failed`. In `create_local_worker_workflow()` that is `discover_metadata`, with `discover_dp_info` → `create_worker` → `register_workers` hanging off it — so one failing optional metadata fetch means the worker is never registered, while `handle_pod_event` has already inserted the pod into `tracked_pods` and only rolls that back when `submit()` itself fails.

That is exactly the class this PR's doc comment describes:

> Membership in `tracked_pods` records that an AddWorker job was SUBMITTED, not that it succeeded […] A job that fails after that […] only records a failed `JobStatus`, and nothing untracks the pod.

The causes named there (`detect_connection_mode` exhausting `worker_startup_timeout_secs`, a failing DP discovery, a workflow that never starts) are all comparatively rare. The wfaas one is not: a transient hiccup on a single optional HTTP call to a pod that has just started is enough to trigger it, so in practice it is a frequent producer of tracked-but-unregistered pods rather than an exotic one.

The two changes are complementary and independent, and can land in either order:

- **This PR without #37249** — the failure still happens on every occurrence; the reconcile recovers the pod, but only on a later resync tick.
- **#37249 without this PR** — that particular cause is gone, but an `AddWorker` failing for any other reason, and a pod whose event never arrives because the watch is dead or silently stale, are still unrecovered.

If it would be useful to reviewers, I am happy to extend `forget_lost_registration`'s doc comment here to name the wfaas case alongside the others once #37249's disposition is clear.

rust-lld: error: unable to find library -ltorch_cpu

`require_prebuilt_rust_exts` returns in 0 s — no prebuilt module for the new crate — so `uv pip install -e python[...]` builds it from source, and the linker search path is uv's isolated build environment (`/root/.cache/uv/builds-v0/.tmp*/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib`), where those libraries are not found. The first `main` run showing this is [33414097466](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/33414097466) at 9cf157c25 (#32710, 2026-08-31), and every `main` run since has failed the same way.

@ShangmingCai — your [08-24 note](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/32322#discussion_r3845710700), that membership in `tracked_pods` implies registry membership only if nothing fails in between, is the hole we hit for real on 2026-09-01. During a rolling restart `/model_info` and `/server_info` timed out on pods that had just started, `create_worker` fell back to `UNKNOWN_MODEL_ID`, and under IGW those workers are healthy, listed, and unroutable for the life of the router process — a *registered* worker is never revisited by discovery. Part of the fleet was silently out of rotation until we deleted the workers by hand. Filed as #37554.

#37555 is the fix for that fallback, and it **depends on this PR**: refusing to register is only safe if something re-submits the pod afterwards, which is `forget_lost_registration` here and does not exist on `main`. It stays in draft until this merges.

In our fork, which carries this PR, a canary ran both arms against stub workers with metadata hanging from boot. With today's code the workers stay `model_id: "unknown"` even after they begin answering; with the refusal they register under their real model name within 18 s — one `--service-discovery-resync-secs 10` tick plus the `AddWorker` that follows it.

The wfaas half of the same story, #37249, is already merged.

Split this into three to make it reviewable, and rebased onto current `main`. This PR is now one production file (`service_discovery.rs`) plus its tests, squashed to a single commit.

The two parts that reached shared subsystems are out, each independently reachable without service discovery at all:

- **#38523** — `WorkerRegistry::register` appends to the secondary indexes, so re-registering a URL leaves the old worker routable in `model_index` and makes `get_by_type(Prefill)` return the decode worker. Reachable via `POST /workers`.
- **#38524** — the add/remove handoff race at the registry, which is where I'd expect the design discussion (the in-flight signal is global rather than per-model).

Keeping those here meant one 20-commit PR touching three subsystems, where two of them changed behaviour for users not on k8s discovery.
